topics.title: Scope and closures
topics.why: Interviewers ask about closures more than almost anything else; learn them at the level of “I can explain it.”
topics.summary: Where a variable can be used, and how a function keeps using the variables from the place it was written, even after that code has finished.
objectives: Say where a variable declared with `let` or `const` can be used, and why one name can mean two variables
Explain what a closure is in two sentences, and spot one in real code
Use a closure to keep private state between calls, the way `makeCounter` and `debounce` do

examples.title: A counter with private state
examples.takeaway: Both methods close over the same `count`, and nothing else can reach it: `clicks.count` does not exist.

examples.title: Run a function only once
examples.takeaway: `called` and `result` survive between calls because the returned function closes over them. `debounce` and caching helpers work the same way.

examples.title: A closure sees later changes
examples.takeaway: The function keeps the variable, not the value it held when the function was made, so it sees the new greeting.

resources.note: The clearest long explanation: blocks, nested functions and how a function keeps the scope it was made in. Try the tasks at the end.
MDN's guide, with private state built from closures and the classic closure-in-a-loop mistake.
This week's practice: 15 to 20 exercises. Write `makeCounter` and `debounce` from memory before you look anything up.

topics.title: Working with arrays and objects
topics.why: Most day-to-day JavaScript work is reshaping data from an API into what the screen needs: map/filter/reduce, destructuring and spread.
topics.summary: Reshape data from an API into what the screen needs with map, filter, reduce, destructuring and spread, without changing the original.
objectives: Choose between `map`, `filter`, `find`, `some` and `reduce`, and chain them
Pull values out of objects and arrays with destructuring, defaults, `?.` and `??`
Update objects and arrays without changing the originals, the way React state needs

examples.title: From API data to what the screen needs
examples.code:
const players = [
  { name: 'Asha', score: 72, active: true },
  { name: 'Ben', score: 91, active: false },
  { name: 'Chen', score: 85, active: true },
  { name: 'Dara', score: 64, active: true },
];

const leaderboard = players
  .filter((player) => player.active)
  .toSorted((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
  .slice(0, 2)
  .map((player, i) => `${i + 1}. ${player.name} (${player.score})`);

console.log(leaderboard); // ['1. Chen (85)', '2. Asha (72)']
console.log(players[0].name); // 'Asha': the original order is untouched
examples.takeaway: Each step returns a new array, so the chain reads like a recipe and `players` never changes.

examples.title: Build a lookup object with reduce
examples.takeaway: An object keyed by id turns every later lookup into one step, instead of a `find` through the whole array.

examples.title: Update nested data without changing it
examples.takeaway: Copy each level you change and reuse the rest. This is exactly how a React state update looks.

topics.why: React later takes over most of this, so learn the model, not every API.
topics.summary: Find and change elements safely, respond to what users do, and handle a whole list of items with a single listener.
objectives: Find elements and change their text, attributes and classes without `innerHTML`
Explain how an event bubbles, and when to call `preventDefault` or `stopPropagation`
Handle events for a whole list with one delegated listener, and remove listeners cleanly

examples.title: Render a list from data, safely
examples.takeaway: `textContent`, and `append` with a string, both create text nodes, so the second author shows up as harmless text instead of running code.

examples.title: One listener for a whole list
examples.takeaway: One listener handles every delete button, including buttons added after it was set up.

examples.title: Remove every listener at once
examples.takeaway: Every listener added with the signal goes away with one `abort()` call, so there is no list of functions to keep for `removeEventListener`.

topics.title: Async code
topics.why: Promises, async/await, fetch and error handling sit behind every API call.
topics.summary: Load data with fetch, promises and async/await: check for errors properly, show every state, and run independent requests at the same time.
objectives: Explain what a promise is, and read and write code with `async` and `await`
Call an API with `fetch`, check `response.ok`, and show loading, error and success states
Run independent requests in parallel with `Promise.all`, and cancel one with `AbortController`

examples.title: Loading, error and success
examples.takeaway: Every path ends with something on screen: “Loading…” first, then the data or a clear message.

examples.title: In parallel where you can, in order where you must
examples.takeaway: Run requests together when they don't need each other's results, and one after another only when they do.

examples.title: Cancel the old search
examples.takeaway: Aborting the old request means a slow, out-of-date answer can never replace newer results.

topics.title: The event loop
topics.why: One of the topics interviewers ask about most; explain the call stack, microtasks and tasks.
topics.summary: How one thread runs your code, timers, events and promises: the call stack, tasks and microtasks, and why a long task freezes the page.
objectives: Describe the call stack, the task queue and the microtask queue, and how the event loop moves between them
Predict the order of logs from plain code, promises, `await` and `setTimeout`
Keep a page responsive by splitting long work into separate tasks

examples.title: Predict the order
examples.takeaway: A microtask queued by another microtask still runs before the next task, and a timer queued later waits behind the earlier one.

examples.title: A long task freezes the page
examples.takeaway: The browser can only paint after the listener returns, so the user sees three frozen seconds and then “Done”.

examples.title: Give the browser a turn
examples.takeaway: Each `await nextTask()` ends the current task, so the page stays responsive however many rows there are.
